Crashes, crashes, and more crashes. Annoying, right? Let's fix that.

1. Right click on Bully: Scholarship Edition in Steam Library.
2. Hover over Manage in the drop down menu.
3. Click Browse local files.
4. Find the program named Bully. It will have a B icon next to it.
5. Right click on Bully, and in the drop down menu that pops up, click Properties.
6. Another menu will open. On the top section of this menu, click on Compatibility.
7. Check the box that says "Run this program in compatibility mode for:"
8. Click on the text box under the checked box.
9. Select Windows 7 from the drop down menu that pops up.
10. Click Apply at the bottom right of the menu.
11. Start Bully: Scholarship Edition. 
12. NO MORE CRASHES!!!

I want to preface this by saying: Bully is an absolutely PHENOMENAL game that I highly recommend anyone to play, especially if you're already a fan of open world GTA-style games. This review is not for the game Bully itself, but instead for specifically the PC port of the game that's available for purchase on Steam. 

Visually and gameplay-wise, this is a pretty damn good port for an older title in my opinion. It definitely feels like the lighting and textures got a bit of an upgrade since the PS2 era, and there's little to no issues with glitches in the gameplay itself other than the camera getting stuck here and there. The main issue with this port, and the reason why I struggle to recommend it for purchase, is because this game is VERY unstable. The PC port of Bully is infamous in the community for almost being unplayable due to its instability, as the game WILL crash with little to no warning at any point while you're playing, and it will be FREQUENT. The game may crash while loading a new area, while you're loading into a mission, while you're finishing a mission, or even just when you're walking around in the overworld minding your own business trying to get from point A to point B. It's almost impossible to play this game for any amount of time over an hour, if you can even play for that long without it crashing, that's how unstable this build is.

A big part of why the game is unstable as hell is no doubt because it doesn't play with with Windows 10/11, but there's not much that can be done about that since Steam doesn't work on older OS's anymore. There's an avid community of people that have been tirelessly trying to figure out how to keep the game working for longer on a modern OS, which involves a LOT of modding, but even with all the bugfix community made patches and mods the game STILL won't run properly for longer than an hour at best. And, the worst part of all, because the game is so unstable if you attempt to run it in compatibility mode for an OS older than Windows Vista and/or run it in admin mode to assist its stability, the game will refuse to allow you to register any controllers plugged into the computer, which is far and away the optimal way to experience this game as the keyboard and mouse controls are absolutely ATROCIOUS, especially when you're using vehicles like the skateboard and bike.

TLDR: Bully is a GREAT game, with great gameplay, fun characters, a banger soundtrack, and a fantastic story. Unfortunately, the PC port (especially on newer machines) is absolutely awful. If you can find another way to play this game that doesn't involve playing it on steam, I recommend doing that instead, because this port simply does not work without it crashing every 15 minutes.

Where the Red Dead series is incredibly grounded and the GTA series is occasionally obscene, Bully steers more into the anarchic insanity sometimes found in the worlds or the latter. 

People who state that you are a "Bully" in this title have never played it. The world is far more complex than that, for all it's comical rhetoric on issues with educational system in western countries. You are simply an individual who is caught up in a world of problems, which you are not responsible for. The player, should they choose to Bully anyone, can do so. However, the protagonist (Jimmy) is a neutral party with an often rational way of approaching each situation.

You are an observer in a world that is a parody of real issues we have all faced. 

Returning to this title, in adulthood, allows for cathartic reflection. If anything, this title is a positive challenge which playfully puts widely ignored issues under a magnifying glass.

BUYERS BEWARE.

 Bully: Scholarship Edition is a slightly updated version of the original 2006 Bully game. Scholarship Edition was released in 2008 on the next gen platforms at the time (PS3, Xbox 360, Wii) and adds some additional content and fixed some bugs as well. Bully, in essence, is the Grand Theft Auto games but if you were a kid. You play as Jimmy a new student at Bullworth Academy, a private boarding school. From here the antics ensue as you work your way from new student to king of the school, earning respect from the various cliques along the way. There are around 75 or so missions to complete throughout the open world and what I found entertaining with this game was the day/night cycle and the aspects related to it. Every day you have 2 classes to attend or not attend it's up to you (though I do recommend getting a few classes under your belt early on as passing each class gives you special perks/abilities that come in handy throughout the game). This along with the repercussion of staying out too late at night (you pass out after 2am and lose all your items) adds a nice wrinkle to the gameplay that I wasn't used to, having only played a few GTA games before this where the day/night cycle doesn't have too much of an affect on the player or gameplay. Being able to fulfill the fantasy of being the bully at school, causing chaos, running rampant throughout the halls, pushing kids in lockers, spraying paint on the walls, running from authority is what this game is all about. As the main story progresses the town of Bullworth gradually opens up to you and you can fully explore the open world Rockstar North created. This game may show it's age graphically and in certain gameplay moments, but overall it was definitely a fun experience.

One of the best sandbox-style games I've ever played! Bully beautifully weaves tweaked Grand Theft Auto gameplay with the universally relatable life story of young Jimmy Hopkins. The setting of a fictional New England boarding school and the nearby town of Bullworth are perfect for this kind of story, following Jimmy as he faces the same challenges that every kid faces growing up, like keeping up with schoolwork, fighting back against bullies, experiencing your first kiss, causing chaos through pranks and hijinks, and finding acceptance between various cliques and social groups.

The writing is brilliant, supplying a colorful cast of characters, missions, and story arcs. Including Jimmy himself, all of the NPCs seem practically handcrafted with the amount of personality and detail put into them. Each character has a unique model, and their own unique set of dialogues and animations. On top of these fantastically created characters, the plot is just as good. I was immersed into a world that I could have sworn was from an 80's Hollywood flick, drawing inspiration from coming-of-age tales like those of Sixteen Candles, The Breakfast Club, and Catcher in the Rye. With such a wonderfully realistic world full of jocks, preps, nerds, and other odd townfolk, I almost wish that my own school days growing up were as interesting as those of Bullworth Academy.

The gameplay is just as entertaining, using similar mechanics to GTA, such as a wanted system (called Truancy, of course), a combat system filled with a diverse array of punches, throws, and weapons at your disposal, different vehicles, mini-games, and other various activities and collectibles for completionists. As usual, there are missions given by various NPCs, some advancing the main story, and others being small side activities. Camera angles can be strange at times, but I've never experienced any gamebreaking issues with it. Overall, the gameplay has enough variance where it doesn't get too repetitive, and it strikes a nice balance that makes it both interesting and easy to pick up.

Compared to other open-world games, Bully is by far my favorite. One of the few titles I've been compelled to complete 100%. If you're looking for something different in the same vein of games such as Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row, and the like, I highly recommend looking into Bully: Scholarship Edition. You won't be disappointed.

[h1]DISCLAIMER[/h1]
[b]You should only purchase Bully: Scholarship Edition if the following statements apply to you:[/b]

1. You already have a controller or can buy one. Playing this game with mouse and keyboard is the most suitable definition of the word [i]"chore"[/i] – and that's coming from a lifelong mouse-and-keyboard player. Controlling the camera and aiming with a mouse will feel horribly unresponsive, and the button layout is so confusing at first that you'll need to spend half an hour setting everything up. Moreover, if you don't have an Xbox gamepad, be ready to perform a little shaman dance and tinker with different settings to get the game to register your controller inputs. Don't worry though – if [i]I[/i] could do it, you can, too.

2. You're okay with downloading and installing third-party software to prevent the game from crashing every five minutes and erasing your progress. Link: [url=https://github.com/CookiePLMonster/SilentPatchBully/r..]Silent Patch.[/url] Setup instructions are located in [b]ReadMe.txt[/b] and are pretty straightforward; your grandma could do it even without her glasses. I would strongly advise against playing Bully without this patch unless for whatever reason you think you deserve to suffer and want to mentally torture yourself, in which case I'd recommend seeing a specialist.

[h1] Too Long; Didn't Read [/h1]
> A large game deserves a large review. For those who want a quick description without delving too deeply into details: Bully is up there with Saints Row and (maybe) Sleeping Dogs; it has all the breakneck fun of the GTA series that you're so familiar with minus the trademark starchy seriousness of a convoluted criminal drama.

[h1] Completion Time [/h1]
> Finishing the main story will take you about 15 hours, and almost twice as long if you're planning to go for [b]100%[/b]. I'm not the fastest player in the world and I like exploring every nook and cranny, not necessarily doing something that contributes to the completion percentage, and I was done with the game in 33 hours. About forty minutes were spent grinding the same repetitive jobs to get the money to buy some fancy clothes, but this is what we do in real life every single day, so you should be okay with that. The rest of playtime is quite varied, exciting and rarely gets old.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2528057948
[h1] Cutscenes | Missions | Classes [/h1]
> When I saw the first cutscene, I immediately fell in love with the characters. Most of them [spoiler](all of them)[/spoiler] are douchebags, yes, but the dialogues, the animation and the voice acting are such treats that you can't help but put your controller down, sit back and enjoy each cutscene like a great 30-second movie.

> There are 52 Story Missions, 24 Side Missions and 50 Errands. They are usually awesome, but some are questionable to say the least. For instance, you'll be delivering what looks like drugs to different people around the area, taking pictures of showering girls for a horny teenager, or, worst of all, collecting dirty laundry from the girls' dorm for an old pervert who will obviously use it for his own nefarious purposes. You can also participate in sedating a clueless Chemistry teacher. He is then [spoiler][i]raped by the school's cooking lady[/i][/spoiler] who promises to show him everything she knows about chemistry... and biology. Enjoy your wicked adventures.

> You can attend classes twice a day; they are small mini-games which are pretty cool: dissecting animals, making words from jumbled letters, playing percussion instruments, painting naughty pictures of your art teacher, Ms Philips, and so on. You should never skip classes because they give pretty cool rewards; for instance, you'll be able to see all collectibles on your map after finishing the Geography course.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2519323348
[h1] Soundtrack | Sound Quality [/h1]
> I loved most songs, they fit the game's atmosphere pretty well, but there is one big issue – most of them feel like they are 15-second loops, and if a mission is particularly long, the music can just stop and you'll be left finishing your exciting bike race in deafening silence.

> The first time I played Bully in my headphones, I was taken aback by the poor sound quality that was not noticeable before. You get used to it pretty quickly though, so no worries. What you will never get used to are shrill, maddening car horns that [u]pierce your eardrums[/u] and most likely give you cancer. I have never heard such annoying noises in my entire life; imagine a toddler screaming at the top of their lungs – it's like Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata compared to the car horns in this game. I was genuinely afraid of riding my bike in the road because of this, and I can't fathom how anyone thought it was a good idea to put a secret state-of-the-art CIA torture device in a videogame.

[h1] Graphics [/h1]
> Most things are quite pleasant to look at, except for Edna the cook – you'll understand. Overall, the visuals in Bully have this special charm of an oldish childhood game you used to play with your brother, but now you don't talk that much anymore and he lives in another city with his wife and two kids. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2521358322
[h1] Carnival | Races | Jobs [/h1]
These are the three main activities you can engage in apart from completing missions and errands.

> The travelling carnival is one of the coolest things in Bully. There's a shooting range, a couple of rides and other standard carnival diversions. You can win tickets and use them to buy awesome things like room decorations or a scooter to zoom around town. 
  
> Speaking of [i]zooming[/i], there are 14 bike races and 8 go-cart races to complete. Most of them are boring, many follow the same path with very minor variations. Your opponents are very easy to overtake, but they're scripted to be tailgating you for the entirety of the race, never letting you relax even for a brief moment. A certain jankiness is present when driving a scooter or a go-cart; your vehicle will constantly jitter back and forth just a little as if having a seizure. This is not the case with bikes, and not a problem when you get used to it, but it does spoil the overall impression a bit.

> Unfortunately, jobs offer very little variation as well – it's either delivering papers or lawn mowing. Each job has 3 stages, but they're all the same – the only difference is in the requirements. This is pure tedium, but you'll be doing it anyway because you need the money; which, once again, should be nothing new for most of us. 

[h1] Clothes, Haircuts and Tattoos [/h1]
> There are 4 clothes shops in Bully, and you'll need upwards of $3000 to buy everything, which is a lot of money in the game where you get $30 on average for completing a mission. You can also give Jimmy (the protagonist) different haircuts and he can even have tattoos; the latter are very hard to actually see while playing or during cutscenes. The customisation options are pretty nice and varied though, and I enjoyed shopping a lot.

[h1] Collectibles [/h1]
> [b]75[/b] rubber bands, [b]40[/b] Grottos & Gremlins cards, [b]25[/b] garden gnomes and [b]6[/b] transistors – have fun collecting them all! Most are in plain view, but some are tucked away or located in areas where you'll only be able to go near the end of the game. That's why you shouldn't trust a midget lady who tasks you with destroying 25 garden gnomes, [i]saying that they're all located in Old Bullworth Vale[/i] – one of the starting areas. This is simply not true. She's trying to bamboozle you and promises to pay as well, but you won't get any money actually, so don't get your hopes up. 

[b]In conclusion, Bully was great, even with its little flaws. Try it out![/b]

Welcome to Bullworth Academy. You play as a 15 year old thug of a kid named Jimmy Hopkins in this third person open world beat-em-up. Sure you get plenty of weapons like the slingshot, eggs, stink bombs that prevent enemies from attacking, firecrackers, a potato cannon and even a bottle rocket launcher, but you'll be spending most of your time brawling. The game is Bully, but you're more of an avenging angel. Sticking up for the weak, but following missions from pervert teachers, and the local crazies. Its the characters in Bully that really make the game stand shoulder to shoulder with Grand Theft Auto games. There is also plenty to do outside of the story missions. Bike races, collect-a-thons, arcade games that are worthy of their own games, classes that are really mini games that will unlock things for you and even a camera so you can take photos of every dumb thing you'll see. Instead of mayhem and murder like the GTA franchise, Bully is more of criminal mischief and knocking people unconscious. You don't even brutally win fights, enemies just fall over. You can finish them off with a childish noogie, putting them in a headlock and spitting on them or one of the many other silly ways.

The game plays similar to Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas meets the Warriors. You have jump and run buttons. An attack that you can hold for a strong attack. A target lock on for projectile weapons. If you don't have one equipped, it becomes a block button when you're not attacking. A free aim button for your sling shots, eggs and so on. A grapple button for when enemies block. You can shove someone when grappled. A taunt button that you can also take them down if grappled. Its a nice simple combat system. A local bum will teach you better attacks when you find and bring him radio parts. Your wrestling coach will teach you grapples in class. The items in your inventory are easy to select on the fly. You can also pick up things like bats and bricks to use and throw. You can even make peace by talking or bribing your way out of things. When you need health, just drink a soda or find some food.

The game is broken up into chapters, the first chapter takes place exclusively in the academy, but chapter two opens the gates and lets you into the rich side of town. Chapter three unlocks the poor side of town and chapter five unlocks a large industrial side of town. There's not only a sense of progression from parts of the town opening up, but the game takes place over a year and you'll see the seasons change. You'll participate in Halloween, slide around in the winter and see spring return.

Each chapter focuses on a faction and there are plenty of them. Nerds in green, bullies in white, greasers in leather jackets, preps in aqua berry and jocks in blue. Each faction has their own turf at the academy, and outside the academy as well. There are even factions outside of academy that will rise against you. All factions have a respect level for you. The less respect, the more likely the members will chase after you wanting a fight! Story missions will always change a faction's respect for you. Sometimes a little, sometimes a lot.

Since this is an open world game you'll be doing a lot of traveling. The main way is by foot. You need to mash the run button to go fast. The enemies all run as fast as you do, but luckily they have stamina and Jimmy doesn't. You quickly unlock a skateboard that sits in your inventory. Its much quicker, but can't go upstairs without a sweet jump or over muddy terrain. There are also bikes, but the bikes feel few and far between. You can throw someone off a bike and steal it, or you can buy a bike, but then it sits in a garage, making it useless when you need to visit a garage in town when you're at the school most of the time. Other than that, you can ride lawn mowers and mopeds. It all feels like a balance. To get speed you button mash. If you're on a lawn mower you're stuck going slower than walking. If you're on a moped you need a helmet or the cops will be after you.

Speaking of laws, there are plenty. You have typical laws against violence, but there are also truancy and curfew laws too. The game lets you know what your offense is on a three step 'wanted' level. When your wanted level hits red, then you can't struggle against the authorities. When they catch you that's it. On campus there are perfects, that act like the police. They'll bring you to class if you're truant, chase you for a dress code violation like wearing a chicken head and stop you from bullying. Sometimes them bringing you to class is more efficient than running to it. When you're in violation, you'll see not only the authorities highlighted on the mini map, but their vision cones. The game makes use of stealth on some missions, but for the most part, its just avoiding the gaze of the cops and perfects. You can even hide in lockers, the trash or dressers in the girl's dorm.

The game is really set to a timetable that can sometimes break the flow. You wake up in the morning and have two classes in the day. You need to find a bed to sleep and if it gets too late, Jimmy will fall asleep where he is and wake up the next day. You can skip classes, but then the authorities will be after you. I felt stuck and forced to partake in the mini games. I want to point out that the class mini games are entertaining and some are educational, but having them forced upon you when I'm trying to do a mission seems a bit much. You can learn things from the game. Such as the flags to different countries in geography, a boggle like make a word with letters in English and even how to dissect animals in biology. I'm not saying this will replace schools by any means. There are also typical timed button press mini games that are less impressive. The game offers a wide array of mini games, even games that parody other games, such as Paperboy, Punch Out and dodge ball! There are even random people that will give you side jobs, like throw 3 nerds in lockers, deliver 3 fries, collect 5 crabs, and so on. All fluff.

The money feels useless. You can spend it on weapons, but why bother when he has an arsenal in his dorm room from completing mini games? There are expensive clothes to buy and tattoos, but why bother other than for cosmetic reasons? Sometimes the game forces you to dress a certain way or get your hair done at the barber shop. You can't buy real estate, even if you can clear out a gang hideout to make it a new save point safe house.

There are dozens of characters in the game. In fact every random person has a name and schedule. You can even take pictures of all of them for the yearbook. Most of the characters are downright evil with a few exceptions. Garry, the over the top villain with an eye scar that lies to cause trouble. Petey, the short effeminate best friend. The drunk Santa. The alcoholic English teacher. The two timing dame that uses men. Russell the big dullard so dumb he calls himself Russell. Its all done in a tongue in cheek 1950s stereotype. The game feels very 1950s even with its awful happy beach guitar riffs. It didn't take me long to turn turn the music down to 10%.

I managed to sink around 17 hours into this game, but I've gotta be honest, I wanted to be done a long time ago. I just spend too much time traveling and wasting too much time doing mini games. At some point I stopped going to class just so I could grind through the missions efficiently. Then the missions started getting further and further. Consuming more precious time that Jimmy is awake during the day. Doing missions back to back so late just means that Jimmy would fall asleep on the street. There are also a few game breaking bugs that would cause the game to freeze or downright crash. Not frequent, but at specific points. I still recommend the game for an open world mischief sandbox that lets you do wedgies, throw firecrackers in toilet and slap kick me signs on people, then watch them get beat to a pulp.

Bully. It's GTA, but without blood and deadly weapons, and instead of playing as an adult man, you play as Jimmy Hopkins. A 15 year old kid who's aggressive and a fighter, but not truly malicious. He only gives people what they have coming to them.

Bully takes place in Bullworth, a town in New England. Your mom, well, Jimmy's mom, drops you off at Bullworth Academy. A boarding school. The school is full of bullies and corrupt teachers and it's up to you to put a stop to it.

The game's storyline will guide you through six chapters. Each of them takes place in a different weather season. The missions vary, it's never the same. One time you're cleaning a rat infested library and the next time you're helping a teacher escape from a psychiatric hospital. As Jimmy, your main goal is to bring peace to the school by helping and befriending the four school cliques: the Nerds, the Jocks, the Bullies, the Preppies and the Greasers.

Of course you'll have to go to class. These classes are: English, gym, geography, math (yuck), music, shop, art, photography and biology. They are simple mini-games which become noticeably harder every time you attend them and make progress. You'll also have to deal with a time schedule. You can skip class, but you won't get any rewards if you do so and prefects will chase you down and send you back to class if they catch you.

Jimmy, your character, is highly customizable. You can buy clothes, change your hairstyle and more. You can even buy a bike, a go-kart or a scooter if you save up enough cash. Money can be earned by either taking a paper route, doing missions for townies or students or by completing storyline missions. 

You've got weapons. No, they are not guns and no you can't kill people. There's a slingshot, you can use firecrackers, stink bombs, eggs, a bag of marbles, a bottle rocket launcher and so much more. You can also pick up one of the many objects around you (umbrella's, vases, bottles) and use them as a weapon.

Interacting with your fellow students is fun too. You can talk to them, give cute presents, put them in trash bins or lockers, steal their books, take their pictures for the yearbook, punch them in their faces and if you feel like it you can make out with a girl or a guy. 

The game has a very impressive map size. You can explore the entire school, the school grounds, the town, a fully functional theme park, an industrial park and a many more awesome places. There are many collectables scattered around the map too.

'Bully' takes place in the town of Bullworth (Which actually exists in the same universe as the 3D 'Grand Theft Auto' games and even 'Manhunt' 1 & 2). Unlike the dull and almost lifeless streets of Liberty City in GTA IV, the town of Bullworth is full of personality and a great deal of variety. You'll experience different seasons as you progress through the story, allowing the player to see Bullworth in the autumn, winter, spring and summer. Even Halloween makes an appearance at one point. Each area is easily distinguishable from the other, and so are the characters. Which brings me to my next point.

What makes the storyline work so well is the witty and likeable nature of all the characters, including the main protagonist. This clever writing even extends to most of the background characters. Hell, even the main antagonist has his moments.

And just like GTA, the further you get into the storyline the more areas and features you unlock.
This is why patience is key when playing through the first chapter. There are 6 chapters. Each Chapter consists of roughly 8 - 15 missions, excluding the 6th chapter because it's basically the "You have completed all of the story related missions, so now you can do any remaining optional sidequests you want"-mode.

The more chapters you complete, the more freedom you're given.
The reason I point this out is because I've seen several people give up halfway through Chapter 1 due to their impatience and an eagerness to explore the environment. Take it easy. Get to know the environment and the characters. I guarantee that you will grow to like the game more if you simply give it time to familiarize yourself with it.

Even the soundtrack is superb. Music composer Shawn Lee's talent really shines here as he shows off a range of different genres and influences.
Don't be surprised if you find yourself humming the 'Walking Tune' when roaming around. My personal favorite song from the soundtrack would be: [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x1XGLtV3Jmo]"Cheating Time."[/url]

I could go on and on about why this game is so likeable, but I think it's about time that we dive into some of the things that don't work so well.

First and foremost, this game performs very poorly on Windows 10. I've seen tons of people come up with all kinds of solutions and compromises to make the game playable, but I've yet to try any of them myself. Some claim that certain fixes work for them, others say they don't. Unfortunately, it seems as though Rockstar has no plans on patching the game for Windows 10.

The game also runs on a 30 fps limit, but there is a mod which removes the framerate cap.
I would suggest installing this mod if you have the game. And while you're at it, why not check out some of the other mods people have made for the game. There are dozens.

Bully may be pretty good, but it's not perfect. The graphics are rather outdated, the sound effects aren't that amazing, the controls are a bit clunky at first (you can tweak them to your liking, luckily enough) and there are some bugs. But don't worry! It doesn't kill the fun. Bully is an amazing game and there's much to do. And for only $14.99 - £9.99 - €9.99, it's certainly worth it.

[b]Rockstar's View On Life In School[/b]

Jimmy is dropped off at a prestigious academy by his mom and the foster dad he despises very much. Our objective, initially, is to try to fit in at the school while the parents are off on their honeymoon. While Jimmy looks like a bully he is in fact bullied by other groups of students so he soon learns there are various factions who all have their own territory. By allying himself with one group he can eliminate another. Divide et impera.

[b]GTA Featherweight Edition[/b]

If you have played at least one GTA game you'll find Bully's gameplay familiar. Shining beacons indicate you can launch a story or secondary mission that is introduced by a cutscene. Voice acting, as usual, is superb. Throughout the story we get to know all the relevant parties at the school: nerds who are afraid of everybody and hide in the library, greasers who show off by oiling their hair and wearing an outdated black jacket, preppies who are the future "fat cats of the town", the athletic jocks who are extremely short on IQ and of course the bullies who are led by Russell, a guy who could easily be called Hulk if his skin colour was just a little closer to green.

If you don't want to do any missions you can just walk around and do pranks on students, try to kiss girls (make sure you have a box of chocolate or a bouquet of flowers at hand), participate in sports activities and, of course, attend classes. These sometimes require you to pick the right answer (math), do some QTE (chemistry, music or shop classes) or go to town and take photos of the local scenery or known monuments (photography). As you progress in your studies the game slowly reveals all collectibles on the map and you are provided with different perks that ease the gameplay.

[b]Open World Done Right[/b]

Exploring the school and its surroundings with the dormitories, the garage, the library and the gym hall is already quite exciting, however, the game goes further and gives Jimmy the opportunity to visit the local town. You know you have reached a new chapter in the game when a new district becomes accessible. Missions are expanded upon: teachers ask you to go to town and buy stuff for them and you meet a new faction (the townies) that represents an even bigger challenge.

You can do chores in the more posh areas of the town (such as becoming the paper boy or mowing the lawn) and participate in bike races. Shops are available for you to buy a better, faster bike and you can also purchase clothes and have your hair cut. Some of these activities are very similar to the ones encountered in San Andreas. By completing challenges you can acquire a building - a place where saving, sleeping and recharging your weapons are a good opportunity. 

[b]Day-Night Cycle Matters[/b]

At 9 AM and 1 PM your classes begin. I do not believe they are mandatory to be attended, however, I liked these minigames so much that I never missed one. As time progresses you soon realise its nightfall and you notice some new missions have become available. Late in the evening the prefects keep searching the school and its areas to see who's violating curfew. Unlike fellow students, you cannot beat up the prefects (the same goes for townsfolk), so unnecessary violence leads to the principal's office. It doesn't mean game over - actually, it's fun mowing the lawn at school as a punishment. Hitting girls is also severely punished (while hitting on them is encouraged and it yields us a health bonus).

Make sure you keep track of time otherwise you'll miss out on missions and fail to attend classes. Also, staying up late for too long (around 2 AM) results in Jimmy's collapsing. Going to sleep is a must in this game. 

[b]Activities At Large[/b]

Numerous activities are available for you as you stroll around on the campus. It's fun looking for collectibles in the girls' dormitories as you know you are trespassing and you'll be kicked out immediately if caught. You can play dodgeball and beat the jocks you hate so much. Students often run up to you and request you to run some errands: this means, for instance, egging the building of a faction or lock picking some of the lockers at school. Even teachers give you tasks - one is a drunkard who wants you to collect all bottles of alcohol at school while the other wants you to fix a date for her.

Riding a bike or skateboarding both allow for faster travel especially when you go to town. At bus stations you can basically fast travel back to campus. I liked how I could do skitching while skateboarding just like Marty McFly. Our favourite gun will include an accurate slingshot with indefinite ammunition and a bottle rocket launcher for swiftly eliminating a group of bullies. The spud gun is basically Bully's equivalent of a pump-action shotgun. We can also use a lot of melee weapons (such as baseball bats) when the going gets tough.

[b]Heaps of Fun, No Gore[/b]

There is a reason why I used the term "Featherweight Edition" above. Bully includes no gore, no extreme violence and is toned down when it comes to cursing. Considering the dialogues and the gameplay it is still a game meant for grown-ups, though. Just because it is a toned-down version of GTA it doesn't mean it's not fun. Quite the contrary! Some of the missions are creative and a joy to play - since driving is replaced by skateboarding and riding a bike I did miss the opportunity to listening to the radio.

[b]Crashes, Crashes Everywhere[/b]

Unfortunately, Bully crashes a lot on modern PCs with particular emphasis on Windows 10. I was 15 hours in the game when completing the mission "Defender of The Castle" the game started crashing in every 15 minutes or so. I noticed launching it in compatibility mode (Windows XP SP 3) helped tremendously. The last 5 hours or so were done without one single crash. Still, reading on this topic in the forums does not confirm that this is a solution for everybody.

[b]A Great Addition To The GTA Roster[/b]

Bully is a great game. It has lots of missions and playing a GTA-like game from a student's perspective is just great fun. It wouldn't be a proper Rockstar game if it hadn't had its fair share of controversial moments. Upon its release roughly 10 years ago not everybody liked the fact that the game included a lot of bullying and kissing your own gender was a possibility. The Scholarship Edition of the game is basically a revamped version of it. If discounted this is a great purchase if you like GTA and / or sandbox games and searching for solutions for crashes is not a deterrent factor for you.

REQUIRES A THIRD-PARTY PATCH!

Don't let that discourage you.

Bully isn't a bad game. It's simply a different experience from Grand Theft Auto or Red Dead Redemption. In many ways, it laid the groundwork for mechanics Rockstar would later expand on in future GTA titles. The game also features a surprisingly large variety of fun mini-games tied to school subjects like English, Math, Chemistry, Art, and Gym, which help give it its own identity.

Yes, you'll likely need a community patch to run the game properly on modern PCs. Thankfully, it's incredibly easy to install. Just download the patch, extract the contents, and place them in the game's root folder.

I understand why some people view this as a negative, but I don't think it's fair to recommend against the game because of it. Plenty of older PC games require community fixes to work reliably on modern hardware. Bully: Scholarship Edition released on Steam in 2008, and expecting Rockstar to continuously update a game that's nearly two decades old for every major Windows and hardware change isn't particularly realistic.

If you're willing to spend two minutes installing a patch, you'll get one of Rockstar's most unique and memorable games. Don't let a simple compatibility fix keep you from experiencing it.
